lesson.title: Functions: Machines That Turn Inputs Into Outputs
lesson.summary: A function is a rule that assigns exactly one output to every input, and function notation, f(x), gives you a precise way to name that rule and evaluate it, building directly on the linear equations you already know how to graph.
lesson.body:
Think of a function as a machine: you feed it an input, the machine follows a fixed rule, and exactly one output comes out the other side. That last part, exactly one output per input, is the entire definition of what makes a relationship a function rather than just some equation. Every linear equation from the last chapter, y = mx + b, already behaves this way: pick any x, and there is only ever one corresponding y. That means every line you graphed was secretly a function all along, just written with y instead of function notation.

Function notation replaces y with f(x), read as 'f of x,' which does not mean f multiplied by x, it means 'the output of the function f when the input is x.' So instead of writing y = 2x minus 1 as in the previous chapter, you could write f(x) = 2x minus 1, and f(2) would mean 'plug 2 in for x,' giving f(2) = 2(2) minus 1 = 3. The notation is more than cosmetic: it lets you name several different functions at once, f, g, h, and refer to specific input-output pairs without confusion, something plain y cannot do once a problem involves more than one relationship at a time.

Evaluating a function follows the exact order of operations rules from earlier in this course. Take f(x) = 2x squared minus 3x plus 1, and find f(3). Substitute 3 everywhere x appears: 2 times 3 squared minus 3 times 3 plus 1. Following PEMDAS, handle the exponent first: 3 squared is 9, so 2 times 9 is 18. Next, 3 times 3 is 9. Now the expression is 18 minus 9 plus 1, which works out left to right to 10. So f(3) = 10, meaning when this function receives the input 3, it outputs 10.

Two more ideas round out the basics: domain and range. The domain is the complete set of inputs a function is allowed to accept, and the range is the complete set of outputs it can produce. For most of the functions in this course, especially straightforward linear and polynomial ones like f(x) = 2x squared minus 3x plus 1, the domain is all real numbers, since there is no input that breaks the rule. Functions matter well beyond this chapter: the entire idea of a limit, and later a derivative, is really a question about how a function behaves as its input changes, so a solid grip on function notation now will make those advanced topics far more readable later.
